c.tagline: Jordan's Red Sea gateway - coral reefs, desert forts, and the road to Wadi Rum and Petra.

taxi.fareNote: Yellow metered taxis are the main way around town; ask the driver to run the meter (addad) or agree a fare first. There is no Uber, and Careem coverage is limited, so most rides are street-hailed or arranged by your hotel.

emergency.note: 911 is Jordan's unified emergency number for police, ambulance, and fire.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Touts around the souk and public beaches can be persistent, and women often prefer private beach clubs to avoid stares.

hood_desc: The historic heart around Aqaba Fort, the giant flagpole, the souks, and the public corniche - cheap eats, local markets, and budget hotels. Best for first-timers who want culture, street food, and value on the doorstep.

The in-town beachfront hotel strip just south of the center where the big five-stars line a private-beach promenade; you get resort comforts while staying walkable to downtown's markets and restaurants.
The stretch of coast along the road toward Tala Bay, home to Aqaba's marine park, dive centers, and the best shore-diving reefs; quieter and focused on snorkeling and diving.
A self-contained luxury beach-resort enclave about 15 km south near the Saudi border, with calm swimming beaches, water sports, and all-inclusive resorts; secluded and family-friendly.
A modern man-made lagoon and marina community on the north edge of town with a golf course, yacht berths, and new-build resorts and residences; polished, walkable, and quiet.
lodging: Mövenpick Resort & Spa Tala Bay Aqaba
Al Manara, a Luxury Collection Hotel

water.note: Stick to bottled or filtered water; tap quality is inconsistent.

transit.hours: Local transport runs roughly dawn to evening; after dark, yellow taxis are the reliable option.
transit.note: Aqaba is compact and mostly navigated on foot in the center or by cheap yellow taxis; local minibuses and buses serve outer districts and intercity routes, but there is no rail or metro.
transit.pay: Minibus and bus fares are paid in cash to the driver (a few piastres to under 1 JOD); taxis run on a meter or an agreed fare.

bus: JETT and Trust intercity coaches to Amman (~4-5h) and Petra
ferry: AB Maritime fast ferry and car ferry across the Gulf of Aqaba to Nuweiba, Egypt

transit.m: Local bus/minibus toward the city center (~20 min, infrequent)
Taxi to the city center or corniche hotels (15-20 min)

tip.r: A 10% service charge is often added to restaurant bills; leaving another 5-10% for good service is customary.

food.name: Sayadieh
food.desc: Aqaba's signature dish: Red Sea fish baked over rice cooked in caramelised onion stock, finished with toasted pine nuts, almonds and tahini sauce.

places.name: Ali Baba Restaurant
places.note: Family-run town-centre institution known for fresh Red Sea fish and generous portions at fair prices.

places.name: Captain's Restaurant
places.note: Nautical-themed seafood house long rated among Aqaba's most reliable fish kitchens.

places.name: Al Shami Restaurant
places.note: Classic Jordanian and Syrian kitchen, good for sayadieh with a full mezze spread.

food.name: Grilled Red Sea fish
food.desc: Whole hamour, sea bream or red mullet landed that morning, salted and grilled over charcoal with lemon, chilli and a plate of tahini-dressed salad.

places.name: Ali Baba Restaurant
places.note: Mixed seafood grills are the house speciality; pick your fish from the ice display.

places.name: Red Sea Grill
places.note: Seafront hotel grill with sea views; pricier but consistently well reviewed for its fish.

places.name: Captain's Restaurant
places.note: Whole grilled fish by weight, plus the local shrimp and calamari plates.

food.name: Mansaf
food.desc: Jordan's national dish: lamb slow-cooked in jameed, a tangy sauce of fermented dried yoghurt, poured over rice and shrak bread with almonds.

places.name: Al Shami Restaurant
places.note: Traditional Jordanian kitchen serving mansaf alongside kebabs, hummus and tabbouleh.

places.name: Sheikh Al Hara
places.note: Local favourite for mansaf with meat and rice, plus sarjiya and grilled chicken plates.

places.name: Ali Baba Restaurant
places.note: Keeps mansaf on the Jordanian side of a menu otherwise dominated by seafood.

food.name: Zarb
food.desc: Bedouin barbecue: lamb, chicken and vegetables lowered in a sealed pit oven under the sand and left to smoke for hours until falling off the bone.

places.name: Bedouin Garden Village
places.note: Coast-road camp south of town that digs a proper zarb pit for dinner; popular with divers.

places.name: Wadi Rum desert camps
places.note: An hour inland, and the definitive setting for a zarb dug out of the desert floor.

places.name: Sheikh Al Hara
places.note: In-town option for pit-cooked lamb without the drive out to the desert.

food.name: Mezze
food.desc: A table of small plates: hummus, mutabbal, fattoush, tabbouleh, warm falafel, labneh with olive oil and stacks of hot bread to scoop it all up.

places.name: Al Shami Restaurant
places.note: Big Levantine mezze spreads; order half the menu and share it across the table.

places.name: Kubba Levantine
places.note: Al Manara hotel restaurant giving Levantine mezze a smarter, modern presentation.

places.name: Al-Nahda Street falafel shops
places.note: Cheap hummus and falafel counters that open early and feed the town all morning.

food.name: Maqluba
food.desc: Upside-down: layers of rice, fried aubergine, cauliflower and chicken or lamb cooked in one pot and flipped onto a platter at the table.

places.name: Al Shami Restaurant
places.note: Home-style maqluba served with yoghurt and a chopped salad on the side.

places.name: Sheikh Al Hara
places.note: Authentic Jordanian home cooking at local prices, away from the hotel strip.

places.name: Ali Baba Restaurant
places.note: Reliable maqluba if the group wants something other than fish.

food.name: Mint lemonade
food.desc: Limonana: lemon juice blitzed with fresh mint, sugar and ice into a slushy pale green drink; the standard antidote to Aqaba's heat.

places.name: Ali Baba Restaurant
places.note: Jugs of freshly blended lemon-mint arrive before the food does.

places.name: Bedouin Garden Village
places.note: Served cold on the shaded terrace between dives.

places.name: Al Shami Restaurant
places.note: Fresh juices and lemon-mint alongside the mezze; no alcohol needed.

food.name: Bedouin tea and Arabic coffee
food.desc: Sweet black tea boiled with sage or mint and poured from height, plus cardamom-heavy Arabic coffee served in tiny handleless cups as a welcome.

places.name: Downtown coffee houses
places.note: Old-town cafes where men play cards over tea and cardamom coffee all afternoon.

places.name: Bedouin Garden Village
places.note: Sage tea poured over a fire in the Bedouin tent after the zarb.

places.name: Wadi Rum desert camps
places.note: The classic setting for Bedouin tea, brewed on coals under the cliffs.

landmarks: Aqaba Fort (Mamluk Castle)
A 16th-century Mamluk stronghold stormed by Lawrence of Arabia's forces in 1917, its stone gateway a touchstone of the Great Arab Revolt.
Aqaba Flagpole and Great Arab Revolt Plaza
One of the world's tallest flagpoles flies the Arab Revolt banner 130 metres above the seafront, visible from Israel, Egypt, and Saudi Arabia.
Ayla Ruins
The excavated remains of the early Islamic port city founded around 650 AD, its coral-stone walls and gates lying incongruously beside modern resorts.
Aqaba Church Ruins
Claimed as the world's oldest purpose-built Christian church, this late 3rd-century mudbrick basilica predates even Bethlehem's Church of the Nativity.
Aqaba Marine Reserve
The Red Sea's northernmost coral gardens, where 500-plus fish species shimmer around pristine reefs accessible to snorkellers straight off the beach.
Cedar Pride Shipwreck
A Lebanese freighter deliberately sunk in 1985 on Jordan's coast, now a coral-encrusted diving icon resting photogenically on its port side.
Sharif Hussein bin Ali Mosque
Aqaba's gleaming white central mosque, its elegant minaret and arcaded courtyards glowing softly under evening floodlights.
Aqaba Archaeological Museum
Housed beside the fort in Sharif Hussein's former residence, displaying Islamic-era treasures from Ayla including a famous Quranic milestone inscription.
South Beach (Berenice Coast)
Aqaba's laid-back southern shoreline, where beach clubs, dive centres, and public sands front the clearest water in Jordan.
Aqaba Bird Observatory
A wetland reserve in the Al-Salam Forest just north of the city where up to 390 migratory bird species can be spotted amid reclaimed desert marshland.

train.note: Jordan has no passenger rail serving Aqaba; the only line is a freight phosphate railway, so travel overland is by coach or car.

bus.note: JETT and Trust International run daily air-conditioned coaches from Aqaba to Amman (~4-5 hours) and to Petra/Wadi Musa; cheap local minibuses cover shorter regional hops.

ferry.note: AB Maritime operates fast catamaran and car-ferry crossings from Aqaba across the Gulf of Aqaba to Nuweiba on Egypt's Sinai coast.

full.blurb: The rose-red Nabataean city and its Treasury carved into sandstone cliffs, about 2 hours north - Jordan's must-see wonder.
full.name: Petra

full.blurb: A full-day desert safari through red dunes, rock bridges, and Bedouin camps under some of the clearest night skies anywhere.
full.name: Wadi Rum

half.blurb: Protected reefs and the sunken Cedar Pride wreck just south of town, reached by boat or shore entry for diving and snorkeling.
half.name: Aqaba Marine Park

half.blurb: Calm resort beaches and water sports 15 minutes south near the Saudi border, ideal for a lazy day by the sea.
